headline: Gold Star pilings holding fish on the last of the ebb, porgies stacked deep at Fort Trumbull
subhead: Water's settled into a real summer pattern on the Thames, and the bite window is short but honest if you're there for it.
body_markdown:
There's a spot below the Gold Star Bridge, maybe forty yards downriver of the third pier from the New London side, where the current pinches between two old dolphin pilings and folds back on itself on the last two hours of the ebb. I've fished that seam for twenty years and it still tells you something new every summer. This week it told me the fish are holding deeper than they were in June — eight, ten feet down against the concrete, not up top chasing bait on the surface like they were a month ago. That's your signal the river's shifted into full summer mode.

Water at the mouth is running around 67, 68 degrees, which for the Thames in mid-July is on the cool side of normal — there's a real gradient stacking up across the Sound right now, warmer out west, cooler as you come east toward us, and that cooler water is exactly why the striper bite here has stayed more honest than a lot of the reports coming out of western Long Island. Fish don't need to run and hide from warm water on this end. They're just settling into their summer addresses.

Stripers off the Gold Star pilings have been mostly schoolies and low-slot fish, 22 to 27 inches, taken on the drop of the tide with white bucktails, half-ounce to three-quarter depending on how hard the current's pushing, tipped with a strip of squid. Let it sink to the base of the piling and hop it slow along bottom — don't rip it, these fish aren't chasing anything fast in this water column right now, they're grubbing. I had three fish in forty minutes doing exactly that on Tuesday's outgoing, nothing enormous, but steady enough that I'd call it a real bite, not a fluke afternoon.

Fort Trumbull is where the bigger story is this week, and it's porgies, not bass. The rock pile off the point, in twelve to eighteen feet, has scup stacked up thick enough that a dropper rig with two hooks, size 6 or 8, baited with sandworm or clam, is coming back doubled up more often than not on the last hour of the incoming. That's the tide to fish there — the flow pushes bait up against the rocks and the porgies tuck in tight to feed on it before the current really starts ripping. I watched a guy in a 17-foot skiff limit out on scup there in under ninety minutes Thursday morning, biggest one pushing a pound and a half, which for the Thames is a genuinely nice fish. If you want a cooler full of dinner without much drama, that's your play right now.

Bluefish have shown up in patches off Ocean Beach and out toward Pleasure Beach, chopping bait on the surface in the mornings before the wind builds. Nothing consistent — I'd call it a here-today, gone-tomorrow bite, the kind where you need to be on the water at first light or you miss the window entirely. Small metal, half-ounce Kastmasters or a Hopkins, worked fast through the froth, gets bit. Once the sun's up and the wind picks out of the southwest, which it's been doing most afternoons this week, the blues seem to scatter back down and out toward the deeper water off the harbor mouth.

Blackfish are still shut down for the season here — that's a fall program on the Thames, once the water starts dropping back toward the 50s and the tog move onto the structure around Fort Trumbull and the rock piles off Bartlett Cove. Too early to think about that yet, though I'll say the mussel beds around the fort have been thick this summer, which is usually a good sign for the fall run when it comes.

Current's been the deciding factor more than anything else this week. The Thames moves fast through the narrows by the bridge, and with these lighter July winds the tide is really running the show — fish are stacking on structure during the strong push and scattering on the slack. If you're planning a trip, build it around the tide chart, not the clock. The two hours either side of dead low, when the current is really cranking past those Gold Star pilings, has been the most dependable window for the bass. For porgies at Fort Trumbull, I'd rather have the last of the incoming pushing bait up onto the rocks than fight a slack tide with nothing moving.

Looking ahead, if this cooler, stable water holds through the week, I expect the striper bite off the bridge to stay steady on the outgoing — nothing spectacular, but reliable enough to plan an evening around. The wildcard is the blues; if that southwest wind eases up even a little in the mornings, I'd bet on a longer window at Ocean Beach before they push back out. And keep an eye on bait activity around the fort — if the porgy bite holds this thick into August, we're in for one of the better scup summers the Thames has had in a few years. I'll be out there most mornings with the tide charts and a bucket of sandworms, and I'll let you know what changes.
